questions.question: Why can square 6 always be replaced by 36 anywhere it appears in a Haskell program?
options: Because GHC caches every function call automatically
Because square is pure — its result depends only on its argument and it has no side effect, so the two are interchangeable in every context
Because 36 is a small number and easy to compute
It can't always be replaced — it depends on which module the call appears in
questions.explanation: Referential transparency means an expression can be swapped for its value without changing observable behaviour, anywhere in the program. That property comes from purity: no hidden state, no side effects, same input always gives the same output.
optionFeedback: Caching (memoisation) is an implementation detail some systems add; it is not what licenses the substitution. Purity is what licenses it, whether or not caching happens.
Correct. Purity is exactly the guarantee that lets you swap an expression for its value with no change in behaviour, in any context.
The size of the number is irrelevant — the same substitution argument would hold for square 60000.
It holds everywhere in a pure program, regardless of module — that is the whole point of referential transparency, as opposed to imperative state that varies by context.

questions.question: Why is x = x + 1 not referentially transparent?
options: Because addition is not a pure operation
Because the same text 'x' denotes different values before and after the statement runs, so 'x' cannot be replaced by a single fixed value
Because it produces a type error
Because it only fails to be referentially transparent inside loops
questions.explanation: This is an imperative assignment/update, not a mathematical equation. Before it runs, x means the old value; after, it means the old value plus one. There is no single value you could substitute for every occurrence of x, which breaks the substitution principle referential transparency relies on.
optionFeedback: Addition itself is pure (it's a function of its arguments); the problem is that x is being reassigned, changing what the name 'x' refers to over time.
Correct — this is precisely why Haskell has no assignment statements: a name always denotes the same value once defined, so this kind of 'equation' cannot exist as a definition.
It is not a type error in imperative languages; the issue is semantic (what the name means over time), not a static typing failure.
The problem is inherent to reassignment itself, not specific to loops — a single such statement outside any loop already breaks referential transparency.

questions.question: In the chain for double (double 2), what justifies the first step, double (double 2) = double (2 + 2)?
options: Arithmetic — 2 + 2 was computed to give the next line
The definition of double, applied to the inner call: double x = x + x with x = 2
The inductive hypothesis
Referential transparency alone, with no definition involved
questions.explanation: The inner double 2 is rewritten using the equation double x = x + x with x instantiated to 2, giving 2 + 2. Arithmetic only happens in the next step, when 2 + 2 is evaluated to 4.
optionFeedback: Arithmetic simplifies 2 + 2 to 4 in the next line — this line only rewrites double 2 using its definition, without doing any arithmetic yet.
Correct. This step replaces double 2 by its defining right-hand side, x + x with x = 2, i.e. 2 + 2.
There is no induction anywhere in this reduction — it is a single concrete calculation, not a proof about all inputs.
Referential transparency is what licenses substituting in general, but the specific rule used here is the definition of double — that's what tells you what to substitute.

questions.question: Why can the chain double (double 2) = ... = 8 legally be read from right to left as well as left to right?
options: It can't — reasoning chains are only valid left to right
Because = is symmetric: a definition is a genuine equation usable in either direction, not a one-way assignment
Because GHC evaluates expressions in both directions automatically
Only the last step (arithmetic) can be reversed; the definition steps cannot
questions.explanation: Section 2 makes this the central point: a Haskell definition is an equation, and equations are symmetric. double x = x + x means double x and x + x denote the same thing, so you may rewrite in whichever direction is useful — forwards to evaluate, backwards to recognise a pattern.
optionFeedback: They are valid in both directions precisely because each step is an equation, not a one-way rule — this is the whole point of calling it 'equational' reasoning.
Correct — every step, definition or arithmetic, is licensed by referential transparency and the fact that = is symmetric.

GHC's evaluator does pick one direction (left-hand side to right-hand side) when it runs your program, but the mathematical justification for the chain works in either direction regardless of what the evaluator does.
Arithmetic equalities (2 + 2 = 4) and definitional equalities (double x = x + x) are both ordinary equations, and both are reversible for the same reason.

questions.question: In the proof that length (xs ++ ys) = length xs + length ys, where exactly is the inductive hypothesis used?
options: In the base case, to simplify length [] + length ys
In the inductive step, to replace length (xs ++ ys) with length xs + length ys inside the calculation for (x:xs)
It isn't used anywhere — the proof only needs the definitions of length and ++
In the conclusion, to state that the claim holds for every list
questions.explanation: The inductive step reduces length ((x:xs) ++ ys) down to 1 + length (xs ++ ys), and it is exactly at that point that the inductive hypothesis licenses replacing length (xs ++ ys) with length xs + length ys — that's the one step definitions alone cannot justify.
optionFeedback: The base case only uses (L1) and ordinary arithmetic (0 + length ys = length ys); the hypothesis has nothing to assume yet at xs = [].
Correct — this is the one line in the inductive step, '= 1 + (length xs + length ys) -- inductive hypothesis', that isn't justified by a definition alone.

Definitions alone reduce length ((x:xs) ++ ys) to 1 + length (xs ++ ys); getting from there to 1 + length xs + length ys needs the assumption about the shorter list xs, which is exactly the inductive hypothesis.
The conclusion states the result of the induction; the hypothesis is used inside the inductive step's calculation, one line before the conclusion is reached.

questions.question: Why is it valid to conclude the claim holds for every finite list, once the base case and inductive step are both proved?
options: Because GHC will type-check the claim if it's true
Because every finite list is built up from [] by a finite number of applications of (:), so the base case plus 'each cons preserves the property' covers every one of them
Because testing a few example lists already confirmed it
It isn't fully valid — induction only covers lists up to some fixed length
questions.explanation: This is the structural content of induction over lists: [] is the only base constructor, (:) is the only way to build a longer list, and the inductive step shows the property is preserved by (:). Together, base case + preservation covers every finite list, however long, by a chain of finitely many cons applications.
optionFeedback: Type checking has nothing to do with why the mathematical argument is valid — GHC doesn't check mathematical claims about function behaviour at all.
Correct — this is exactly why induction proves a universal claim rather than a handful of examples: it argues about the two ways any finite list can be built.
Testing gives evidence for specific lists only; the completed induction is what licenses the claim for every list, tested or not.
Induction over lists genuinely covers every finite list, of any length — there is no length cutoff, because the inductive step is proved once and applies at every stage of construction.

questions.question: In the inductive step for sum (map (*2) xs) = 2 * sum xs, which line uses ordinary algebra rather than a definition or the hypothesis?
options: = (x*2) + 2 * sum xs -- inductive hypothesis
= 2 * (x + sum xs) -- distributivity
= sum (map (*2) (x:xs)), the starting expression
questions.explanation: The step '(x*2) + 2 * sum xs = 2 * (x + sum xs)' is a fact about multiplication and addition (a*2 + 2*b = 2*(a+b)), not about the definitions of sum or map, and not the inductive hypothesis (which was already used one line above). It is exactly analogous to the 'associativity of +' step in the length proof.
optionFeedback: This line is justified by (M2), the definition of map on a non-empty list — it's a definitional rewrite, not algebra.
This line is exactly where the inductive hypothesis is used — it's not the algebraic step being asked about.
Correct. Factoring 2 out of (x*2) + 2*sum xs to get 2*(x + sum xs) is a fact of ordinary arithmetic (distributivity), used the same way 'associativity of +' was used in the first proof.
This is the starting expression of the inductive step, not a justified rewrite step at all.

questions.question: How does the structure of this proof compare to the length (xs ++ ys) proof from Section 3?
options: They are unrelated techniques
Both use structural induction over the list with a base case at [] and an inductive step at (x:xs), applying the hypothesis once inside the step and then an algebraic fact to match the target shape
This proof does not need a base case because sum and map are both total functions
This proof uses induction on the second argument, ys, instead of the first
questions.explanation: Both proofs follow the same template shown in the Mermaid diagram in Section 3: base case at [], assume for xs, prove for (x:xs) using the hypothesis, then a small algebraic or definitional rewrite ('backwards' use of a definition, or distributivity/associativity) to land exactly on the target shape.
optionFeedback: They use exactly the same technique — structural induction over the list — just applied to a different claim.
Correct — same shape: base case, hypothesis, inductive step using the hypothesis plus one algebraic fact, then match the target form.
Totality of the functions involved guarantees termination, but it does not remove the need for a base case in the induction — every structural induction over a list needs one, to anchor the argument.
The induction is over xs, the first (list) argument to sum . map (*2), exactly as in Section 3 — there is no second list argument here to induct over.

check-using-reasoning-to-find-a-fault.title: Check: using reasoning to find a fault

questions.question: In the faulty myReverse proof, the inductive step derives myReverse (myReverse (x:xs)) = xs, but the claim needed it to equal (x:xs). What does this mismatch tell you?
options: The proof technique itself is invalid for this function
The definition of myReverse is faulty — specifically, it is missing the operation that would append x back on, and the mismatch (xs vs x:xs) is a one-element gap at exactly that spot
The base case must be wrong instead
Nothing — a failed step just means you should pick a different claim to prove
questions.explanation: The technique is sound; it correctly detects that this definition does not satisfy the claim. The gap between xs and (x:xs) is precisely one cons of x, which is exactly the missing ++ [x] in myReverse's recursive case.
optionFeedback: Structural induction is a valid proof technique regardless of outcome — here it correctly reports that the claim fails for this definition, which is the technique working as intended.
Correct. The one-element gap between the derived xs and the required (x:xs) points exactly at the missing ++ [x] — the proof doesn't just say 'wrong', it says where.
The text states the base case was checked and holds; the failure is specifically in the inductive step, not the base case.
The claim (reverse (reverse xs) = xs) is a true, reasonable property to want — the fault is in the code, not in choosing to prove this particular claim.

questions.question: Why is running myReverse [1,2,3] and seeing [] not, by itself, a proof that myReverse is wrong for every input?
options: It is a proof — one failing test is logically equivalent to a completed induction
A single test (or even several) only shows the function is wrong for the inputs actually tried; it doesn't identify the general pattern the way inspecting the inductive step's algebra does
The test result [] is actually correct, so there's nothing to explain
GHC would have refused to compile a wrong definition, so the test is irrelevant
questions.explanation: This is the running theme of the chapter: testing gives evidence for the inputs tried, not a general argument. It takes inspecting the equations themselves — as the induction does — to see the general shape of the fault (a whole ++ [x] missing) rather than just 'it returned the wrong list for [1,2,3]'.
optionFeedback: One test is evidence for one input; it is not equivalent to an argument covering every possible list, however suggestive the failure is.
Correct — the test shows *that* something is wrong for a couple of inputs; the induction shows *why*, in general, for every input.
[] is wrong — myReverse [1,2,3] should be [3,2,1] once reversed correctly, so [] is a visible symptom of the fault, not a correct answer.
myReverse [1,2,3] compiles and runs fine; the fault is semantic (it computes the wrong value), which is exactly the kind of error GHC's type checker cannot catch.

deeper-reasoning-testing-versus-proof-an.title: Deeper reasoning: testing versus proof, and why substitution is safe

questions.question: A student tests the property below on nine pairs of lists, sees True, and writes: "I have proved that length (xs ++ ys) always equals length xs + length ys." Which assessment of that claim is the most accurate, and what would a proof need to do instead?
code: prop xs ys = length (xs ++ ys) == length xs + length ys
options: The claim is correct: if a property holds for nine well-chosen pairs, Haskell's purity guarantees that it holds for all lists.
The claim is correct, because the test includes the empty list, and the empty list is the only case that can fail.

Nine passing cases are evidence, not proof; they say nothing about the infinitely many other lists. A proof argues about every finite list at once by structural induction on xs, following the same two cases as the recursive definitions. The base case shows that [] ++ ys has the length of ys. The inductive step assumes the claim for xs and shows that it holds for x : xs, using the definitions of ++ and length and the inductive hypothesis.
The claim is wrong, because a property of lists can only be established by testing every list up to length 10.
questions.explanation: A dry run or a test shows what happens for specific inputs. Equational reasoning establishes a statement for every input in a structured family. For lists, the family is generated by [] and (:), so induction over those two constructors covers all finite lists.
optionFeedback: Purity makes substitution reliable, but it does not turn a finite set of tests into a proof about all inputs.
The empty list is a good test but not the only one that can fail. Faults can appear in the step as well as in the base.
Correct. The proof mirrors the structure of the recursive definitions, which is why being able to write the recursion helps with writing the proof.
No finite bound on list length is enough, so exhaustive testing cannot establish the property for all lists. Induction can.

questions.question: A student attempts to explain why a derivation like double (double 2) = double 2 + double 2 = 4 + 4 = 8 is legitimate in Haskell, but would not be in a language where x = x + 1 is a statement. Which explanation is the most accurate?
options: It is legitimate in Haskell because Haskell is faster, so the substitution always happens at run time.

In Haskell, a definition such as double x = x + x is a genuine equation, and an expression such as square 6 can be replaced by its value, or the other way round, without changing what the program means. This is referential transparency, and it holds because the functions are pure: the result depends only on the argument, and evaluation causes no outside-world effect. In a language with assignment, the same text x can mean different things before and after x = x + 1, so replacing an expression by something equal to it is no longer safe.
It is legitimate only for numbers, because every other type changes when its name is reused.
It is legitimate in both kinds of language, because substitution never depends on whether values can change.
questions.explanation: Substitution of equals for equals is only safe if an expression always has the same value in the same context. Purity gives that guarantee, and the guarantee is what makes pencil-and-paper reasoning about programs possible.
optionFeedback: Speed has nothing to do with it. The justification is a property of the language: the meaning of an expression does not depend on when it is evaluated.
Correct. Referential transparency is the licence for each step in an equational proof.
Substitution works for every pure function and every type. Numbers are not special.
In a language with assignment, substitution is not safe in general, because the same expression can have different values at different moments.

questions.question: Two students expand the same expression in different orders, as the program below shows. One replaces the inner call first, the other replaces the outer call first. The second student asks whether their derivation is cheating. Which answer is correct?
options: It is cheating, because the outer call may only be replaced after the inner one has been evaluated.

Both derivations are legal. The definition double x = x + x is an equation that holds for any expression in place of x, so double (double 2) can be rewritten as double 2 + double 2 by substituting the argument double 2 for x, or the inner call can be rewritten first. Both orders lead to the same value, 8, because the functions are pure; each step only needs to be justified by naming the rule used.
Only the second derivation is legal, because substituting the outer call first always requires fewer steps.
Neither derivation is legal, because a definition can be used only after the arguments are fully evaluated.
questions.explanation: A definition is an equation that can be used in either direction and at any position where its left-hand side matches. In a pure language the order of substitution does not change the final value, though it may change the number of steps.
optionFeedback: There is no rule requiring the inner call to be replaced first. The equation applies whenever its left-hand side matches.
Correct. The three printed values agree, and each derivation is acceptable as long as every step is justified.
Legality does not depend on how many steps a derivation has.
Arguments do not have to be evaluated before a definition is applied in a proof. They can be substituted as they stand.
